## Data Generating Process

The simulations are a fully factored experiment. 

**Block Level Fixed Covariates**  
Number of Blocks: 5;  ATE: .2; ICC: .2; Average Number of Observations Per Cluster: 20; Proportion of Clusters Treated: .5 (this is fixed across blocks); Number of District Level Covariates: 0; How much does the average cluster size vary across blocks (coefficient of variation)?: 0

**Block Level Varying Covariates (Factors that are varied across simulations)**

Three groups of block level parameters Blocks all the same, Blocks all messy, and Blocks all reasonable

Blocks all the same: How much do number clusters per block vary (coefficient of variation)?: 0 (none);  ATE SD: 0; Correlation Between Treatment Effect and Cluster Size: 0; Correlation Between Average Number of Observations Per Cluster and Total Number of Clusters: 0; Correlation of Proportion of Clusters Treated per Block and Impact: 0; Correlation Between Outcome Intercept and Cluster Size: 0

Blocks all messy: How much do number clusters per block vary (coefficient of variation)?: .85 (big); ATE SD: .6; Correlation Between Treatment Effect and Cluster Size: .8; Correlation Between Average Number of Observations Per Cluster and Total Number of Clusters: .8; Correlation of Proportion of Clusters Treated per Block and Impact: .8; Correlation Between Outcome Intercept and Cluster Size: .8

Blocks all reasonable: How much do number clusters per block vary (coefficient of variation)?: .33 (average); ATE SD: .1; Correlation Between Treatment Effect and Cluster Size: .2; Correlation Between Average Number of Observations Per Cluster and Total Number of Clusters: .1; Correlation of Proportion of Clusters Treated per Block and Impact: 0; Correlation Between Outcome Intercept and Cluster Size: .1

Each of the rest of these factors don't vary as a group but vary each individually and are fully factored with all other factors:

Average Number of Clusters per Block: 7,10,16

**Cluster Level Varying Parameters**

Correlation of Impact and Size of Cluster: 0, .8

Cluster Level Treatment Effect Standard Deviation: 0, .3

Cluster Level ICC: 0, .2

Number of Observations Per Cluster Varies: True, False 

How much does the size of clusters vary (coefficient of variation)?: 0, .33, .6 

Number of School-Level Covariates: 0, 1, 5

[School Level Covariate R Squared is always .5]


## What does the bias look like for each estimator 


*The next thing to do is to move all the simulation questions I'm answering to my emails and also to attach the page numbers to the analysis 

Main Bullet Points:

*The estimators theory says are unbiased are indeed consistently unbiased (or have very low bias across the full range of simulations)

*The LRapw−FIpw−db has bias as large as -.025, which seems from the statistical model to be driven by the interactions of a large treatment effect standard deviation across clusters, high variability in cluster size, and correlations between treatment effect and cluster size. This is consitent with theory. 

*For the various estimators that are biased, the mean bias is mostly driven by the different blocks being different from each other  


Description of Analysis

*The graph is a boxplot of mean bias across the different scenarios by method. The faint horizontal lines go out to the full range, the bars are the 1% to 99%, and the boxes are the 10% to 90%.

*The first table contains the regression coefficients from a regression that predicts the magnitude of the mean bias using different data generating parameters. Each regression is run separately by estimator and mean bias is the mean bias against the targeted estimator. 

*The second table contains the DGPs that produce that largest magnitude of mean bias for each method, conditional on the magnitude of the mean bias being at least .1 . Where again mean bias is the mean bias against the targeted estimator.

# Create a list to store models
models_by_method <- list()
model_summaries <- list()

# Run separate models for each method
for (m in core.methods) {
  # Subset data for this method
  method_data <- sruns.clean %>% filter(method == m)
  
  # Run the model for this method
  # Note: I'm using bias.s.estimand as you specified in your formula
  # Make sure this column exists or replace with the correct one
  models_by_method[[m]] <- lm(bias.s.estimand.mag ~ (block_type + J.bar + size.impact.cor.school + 
                                                 sd.school + ICC.school + variable.n + 
                                                 cv.school + num.cov.school)^2, 
                              data = method_data)
  
  # Store summary statistics
  model_summaries[[m]] <- broom::tidy(models_by_method[[m]])
  
}


# Helper function to add significance stars
  add_stars <- function(p_value) {
    if (is.na(p_value)) return("")
    if (p_value < 0.001) return("***")
    if (p_value < 0.01) return("**") 
    if (p_value < 0.05) return("*")
    if (p_value < 0.1) return(".")
    return("")
  }


# Function to create a coefficient table with wrapped term names
create_coefficient_table <- function(model_list) {
  # Get all unique terms across all models
  all_terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(model_list, function(m) {
    coef_names <- names(coef(m))
    return(coef_names)
  })))
  
  # Create extraction functions
  extract_coef <- function(model, term) {
    if(term %in% names(coef(model))) {
      return(coef(model)[term])
    } else {
      return(NA)
    }
  }
  
  extract_p <- function(model, term) {
    if(term %in% rownames(summary(model)$coefficients)) {
      return(summary(model)$coefficients[term, "Pr(>|t|)"])
    } else {
      return(NA)
    }
  }
  
  # Function to wrap long term names
  wrap_term <- function(term, width = 25) {
    if (nchar(term) <= width) {
      return(term)
    }
    
    # For interaction terms (with :), try to break at the colon
    if (grepl(":", term)) {
      # Replace ":" with newline character
      wrapped <- gsub(":", ":\n", term)
      return(wrapped)
    }
    
    # Otherwise, use general text wrapping logic
    # Find a good breaking point
    break_point <- width
    while (break_point > 0 && substr(term, break_point, break_point) != " " && 
           substr(term, break_point, break_point) != "_") {
      break_point <- break_point - 1
    }
    
    if (break_point == 0) {
      # If no good breaking point, just break at width
      break_point <- width
    }
    
    # Insert newline character
    wrapped <- paste0(
      substr(term, 1, break_point),
      "\n",
      substr(term, break_point + 1, nchar(term))
    )
    
    return(wrapped)
  }
  
  # Create result dataframe
  result <- data.frame(Term = sapply(all_terms, wrap_term), 
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  # Add coefficients for each method with shorter formatting

  for(m in names(model_list)) {

    coefs <- sapply(all_terms, function(t) extract_coef(model_list[[m]], t))
    p_vals <- sapply(all_terms, function(t) extract_p(model_list[[m]], t))
    stars <- sapply(p_vals, add_stars)
coef_strings <- ifelse(
  !is.na(coefs),
  ifelse(
    round(coefs,3) == 0,
    paste0("<.001", stars),  # Just "0" for zero values
    paste0(
      # Drop leading zero for values between -1 and 1
      sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", sprintf("%.3f", coefs)),
      stars
    )
  ),
  "")
    
    
    # Use abbreviated method names if they're too long
   method_name <- ifelse(nchar(m) > 15, 
                          paste0(substr(m, 1, 14), "."), 
                        m)
    
    # Add to result
    result[[method_name]] <- coef_strings
  }
  
  return(result)
}

# Generate the coefficient table
coef_table <- create_coefficient_table(models_by_method)

# Set row names to NULL
row.names(coef_table) <- NULL

# Add a footnote explaining significance levels
add_significance_footnote <- function(table_object) {
  footnote(table_object,
    general = "Significance codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1",
    general_title = "Note: "
  )
}

# Create comparison table with significance stars - MODIFIED to make narrower output
create_star_comparison_table <- function(model_list) {
  # Initialize a list to store tidy model outputs
  tidy_models <- list()
  
  # Process each model
  for (m in names(model_list)) {
    # Get model coefficients and p-values
    model_stats <- tidy(model_list[[m]]) %>%
      # Create a column with coefficient and stars - USING SHORTER FORMAT
      mutate(
        stars = sapply(p.value, add_stars),
        # Reduce number of decimal places from 3 to 2 to save space
        coef_stars = ifelse(!is.na(estimate),
                            sprintf("%.2f%s", estimate, stars),
                            "")
      )
    
    # Add to our list
    tidy_models[[m]] <- model_stats
  }
  
  # Combine all models into a single data frame
  all_terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(tidy_models, function(x) x$term)))
  
  # Initialize result dataframe
  result <- data.frame(term = all_terms)
  
  # Add each method's coefficients as a column
  for (m in names(model_list)) {
    temp_df <- tidy_models[[m]] %>% 
      select(term, coef_stars)
    
    # Rename to method name - USING SHORTER METHOD NAMES if needed
    # If method names are long, you could abbreviate them here
    # For example: names(temp_df)[2] <- substr(m, 1, 3)  # First 3 chars only
    names(temp_df)[2] <- m
    
    # Join to result
    result <- result %>% 
      left_join(temp_df, by = "term")
  }
  
  return(result)
}

create_top_n_table <- function(data, 
                              column_to_rank_by, 
                              methods_to_include = NULL,
                              n = 5, 
                              abs_value = TRUE, 
                              descending = TRUE,
                              min_threshold = NULL,
                              columns_to_display = NULL) {
  
  # Make a copy of the data
  df <- data
  
  # Convert column_to_rank_by to symbol for dplyr operations
  col_sym <- sym(column_to_rank_by)
  
  # Filter methods if specified
  if (!is.null(methods_to_include)) {
    df <- df %>% filter(method %in% methods_to_include)
  }
  
  # Setup ranking
  if (abs_value) {
    # Use absolute value for ranking
    df <- df %>%
      group_by(method) %>%
      arrange(desc(abs(!!col_sym))) %>%
      slice_head(n = n)
  } else {
    # Use actual value for ranking
    if (descending) {
      df <- df %>%
        group_by(method) %>%
        arrange(desc(!!col_sym)) %>%
        slice_head(n = n)
    } else {
      df <- df %>%
        group_by(method) %>%
        arrange(!!col_sym) %>%
        slice_head(n = n)
    }
  }
  
  # Sort methods alphabetically
  df <- df %>% arrange(method)
  
  # Apply threshold if specified
  if (!is.null(min_threshold)) {
    if (abs_value) {
      df <- df %>% filter(abs(!!col_sym) > min_threshold)
    } else {
      if (descending) {
        df <- df %>% filter(!!col_sym > min_threshold)
      } else {
        df <- df %>% filter(!!col_sym < min_threshold)
      }
    }
  }
  
  # Select columns to display
  if (!is.null(columns_to_display)) {
    df <- df %>% select(all_of(columns_to_display))
  }
  
  # Convert to data frame
  df <- as.data.frame(df)
  
  # Wrap column names
  current_names <- names(df)
  for (i in 1:length(current_names)) {
    if (nchar(current_names[i]) > 7) {  # If name is longer than 7 characters
      # Find a good breaking point (space, underscore, etc.)
      mid_point <- ceiling(nchar(current_names[i]) / 2)
      
      # Look for a space near the middle
      space_pos <- as.numeric(regexpr("[ \\._]", substr(current_names[i], mid_point-2, mid_point+2)))
      
      if (space_pos > 0) {
        # Break at the space
        break_point <- mid_point - 3 + space_pos
        names(df)[i] <- paste0(
          substr(current_names[i], 1, break_point-1),
          "\n",
          substr(current_names[i], break_point+1, nchar(current_names[i]))
        )
      } else {
        # No space found, just break in the middle
        names(df)[i] <- paste0(
          substr(current_names[i], 1, mid_point),
          "\n",
          substr(current_names[i], mid_point+1, nchar(current_names[i]))
        )
      }
    }
  }
  
  
  # Return the data frame
  return(df)
}


result <- create_top_n_table(
  data = sruns.clean,
  column_to_rank_by = "bias.s.estimand.mag",

## What does the error look like for each estimator 

Main Bullet Points:

*For the person weighted estimators, the unbiased estimator both has less error and is more stable than the biased estimator. 

*For the cluster weighted estimators, the unbiased estimator generally has less error than the biased estimators but more instablity. 

*The MLM estimators are the most stable, which fits with theory. 

*High RMSE and estimate instability is driven by a low number of clusters, the interaction of a low number of clusters and high cluster level ICC, and high cluster level treatment effect variance. 

*Re the question on pg. 39, looking at the second boxplot shows that true S.E. do vary across estimators with the true standard error in a given DGP often 40% bigger for some estimates than the median estimate in that DPG. 

Description of Analysis:

*The first graph is a boxplot of the normalized RMSE across the different scenarios by method. The normalized RMSE is the RMSE for given method divided by the median RMSE across methods within a given simulation scenario. Therefore each data point is adjusted for the underlying base RMSE from a given set of DGPs and represents the RMSE driven by the estimation method.

*The second graph is a boxplot of the normalized estimate standard deviation across the different scenarios by method. This is also normalized by dividing by the median estimate standard deviation within a given simulation scenario. 

*The first table contains the regression coefficients from a regression that predicts the RMSE using different data generating parameters and the second table is from regressions predicting the estimate standard deviation. Each regression is run separately by estimator and the RMSE is against the targeted estimator. 

*The second table contains the DGPs that produce the normalized RMSE (against the targeted estimator) for each method, conditional on the magnitude of the being at least 1.10. 

*The third table contains the regression coefficients from a regression that predicts the true superpopulation estimate standard error using different data generating parameters.

*The fourth table contains the five DGPs that produce the most normalized super population estimator standard error for each method, conditional on the magnitude of the being at least 1.10.

## What do the estimated standard errors look like for each estimator

Main Bullet Points:

*This section answers the rest of the questions from pg.39 (i.e. are certain SE estimators more accurate than others) 

*For the cluster targeted estimates the unbiased estimators produce more accurate standard errors than the biased estimators (graph one). The unbiased estimators produce more unstable estimates than the biased estimators, but in 90% of the DGP we looked at they aren't a lot more unstable (graph four).

*For the person targeted estimates the unbiased estimators produce more accurate standard errors than the biased estimators (graph one), except when the school ICC is zero and the blocks are all very dissimilar from each other and their is high variance in the cluster sizes. if all three of these risk factors are not present than the unbiased estimator standard estimates are generally fine (graph two). The unbiased estimators produce more unstable estimates than the biased estimators unless all three of these factors are present (graphs four and five). However they aren't a lot more unstable, 90% of the time they're within about 10% of the median instability. 

*This section also answers the question from pg. 38 about the instability of the estimated standard erros for the fully interacted models, what I've been calling hte unbiased estimators. The simulations do not really show that the standard errors from the fully interacted models are lot more unstable than the other standard errors. We should talk about this more, and what would be helpful for me to dig into more. 


Description of Analysis:

*The first graph is a boxplot of the estimated standard error accuracy across the different scenarios by method. Standard error accuracy is quantified as the estimated standard error over the true super population standard error. Estimated standard errors are most accurate if the number is close to one. Numbers below one represent under estimated standard errors and numbers above one represent over estimated standard errors. 

*The second graph is the same as the first but for just the person weighted fully interacted estimators broken out by identified "risk factors" for poorly estimated standard errors. In the graph on the left the school level ICC is zero, the blocks are all messy, and there is high variance in the cluster size and the graph on the right does not have all three of these things at the same time. 

*The third graph is a boxplot of the standard deviation of the estimated standard error across the different replications by method. 

*The forth graph is a boxplot of the normalized standard deviation of the estimated standard error across the different replications by method. 

*The fifth graph is the same as the fourth graph but broken by the same risk factors as before. 

* I was having trouble conceptualizing the scale of standard error inflation, so for the regression I converted it to percentage inaccuracy. The regression's for table one are therefore predicting the magnitude of ((Mean Estimated SE - True Super Population SE) / True Super Population SE) * 100.  

*The second table contains the five DGPs that produce the most inaccurate standard error estimates for each method, conditional on the magnitude of the inaccuracy being at least .1. 

*The third table contains the regression coefficients from a regression that predicts the standard deviation of the standard errors across simulations using different data generating parameters.

*The fourth table contains the five DGPs that produce the largest standard deviation in the standard error estimates for each method, conditional on the magnitude being at least .05. 

*The fifth table contains the five DGPs that produce the largest normalized standard deviation in the standard error estimates for each method, conditional on the magnitude being at least 1.10.

# Function to create a coefficient table with wrapped term names
create_coefficient_table_wide <- function(model_list) {
  # Get all unique terms across all models
  all_terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(model_list, function(m) {
    coef_names <- names(coef(m))
    return(coef_names)
  })))
  
  # Create extraction functions
  extract_coef <- function(model, term) {
    if(term %in% names(coef(model))) {
      return(coef(model)[term])
    } else {
      return(NA)
    }
  }
  
  extract_p <- function(model, term) {
    if(term %in% rownames(summary(model)$coefficients)) {
      return(summary(model)$coefficients[term, "Pr(>|t|)"])
    } else {
      return(NA)
    }
  }
  
  # Function to wrap long term names
  wrap_term <- function(term, width = 13) {
    if (nchar(term) <= width) {
      return(term)
    }
    
    # For interaction terms (with :), try to break at the colon
    if (grepl(":", term)) {
      # Replace ":" with newline character
      wrapped <- gsub(":", ":\n", term)
      return(wrapped)
    }
    
    # Otherwise, use general text wrapping logic
    # Find a good breaking point
    break_point <- width
    while (break_point > 0 && substr(term, break_point, break_point) != " " && 
           substr(term, break_point, break_point) != "_") {
      break_point <- break_point - 1
    }
    
    if (break_point == 0) {
      # If no good breaking point, just break at width
      break_point <- width
    }
    
    # Insert newline character
    wrapped <- paste0(
      substr(term, 1, break_point),
      "\n",
      substr(term, break_point + 1, nchar(term))
    )
    
    return(wrapped)
  }
  
  # Create result dataframe
  result <- data.frame(Term = sapply(all_terms, wrap_term), 
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  # Add coefficients for each method with shorter formatting

  for(m in names(model_list)) {

    coefs <- sapply(all_terms, function(t) extract_coef(model_list[[m]], t))
    p_vals <- sapply(all_terms, function(t) extract_p(model_list[[m]], t))
    stars <- sapply(p_vals, add_stars)
coef_strings <- ifelse(
  !is.na(coefs),
  ifelse(
    round(coefs,3) == 0,
    paste0("<.001", stars),  # Just "0" for zero values
    paste0(
      # Drop leading zero for values between -1 and 1
      sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", sprintf("%.3f", coefs)),
      stars
    )
  ),
  "")
    
    
    # Use abbreviated method names if they're too long
   method_name <- ifelse(nchar(m) > 15, 
                          paste0(substr(m, 1, 14), "."), 
                        m)
    
    # Add to result
    result[[method_name]] <- coef_strings
  }
  
  return(result)
}

# Set row names to NULL

## Are the estimated standard errors targeting the finite or super population

*This section answers the questions on page 8.

*As long as the school level ICC isn't zero, than the true finite and super population standard errors are very similar to each other (graph 2). 

*I was having a little trouble visualizing whether the standard errors were targeting the finite population or super population standard errors, so I made up this metric: difference in % inaccuracy. This is calculated as the magnitude of ((Mean Estimated SE - True Super Population SE) / True Super Population SE) x 100 minus the magnitude of  ((Mean Estimated SE - True Finite Population SE) / True Finite Population SE) x 100. When this number is positive the estimated standard errors are closer to the true super population standard errors and when this number is negative the estimated standard errors are closer to the finite population. 

*The only estimators with standard errors that are ever really significantly closer to the finite standard errors than the super population standard errors are the person weighted fully interacted one's and the fully interacted MLMs (graphs three and four). It does look like the person weighted fully interacted estimators are targeting the finite standard errors when the ICC is zero, the blocks are very dissimilar, and there is high variance in the cluster sizes. Otherwise these estimators are also targetting super population standard errors (graph five).  


Description of Analysis:

*The first graph is a boxplot of ratio of the true finite standard errors over the true super population standard errors across the different scenarios by method. When this metric is one the two standard errors are the same, when it's above one the finite population standard errors are bigger and when it's below one the super population standard errors are bigger. 

*The second graph is the same as the first but broken out by ICC. In the graph on the left the school level ICC is zero and on the right it's .20.

*The third graph is a boxplot of the difference in % inaccuracy across methods. This is calculated as the magnitude of ((Mean Estimated SE - True Super Population SE) / True Super Population SE) x 100 minus the magnitude of  ((Mean Estimated SE - True Finite Population SE) / True Finite Population SE) x 100. When this number is positive the estimated standard errors are closer to the true super population standard errors and when this number is negative the estimated standard errors are closer to the finite population. 

*The fourth graph is the same as the third but broken out by ICC. In the graph on the left the school level ICC is zero and on the right it's .20.

*The fifth graph is a boxplot of the difference in % inaccuracy across methods, but only for the methods that might be targeting the finite population standard errors and only when the school level ICC is zero, the blocks are all messy, and the cluster size coefficient of variation is large. 

*The table contains the five DGPs that produce the largest difference in % inaccuracy for each method, conditional on the magnitude being at least five percentage points.

## What do the confidence intervals look like for each estimator 

Main Bullet Points:

*Coverage is the percentage of simulation replications where the estimator is within the 95% confidence interval. We would like the number to 95% (the boxplots have a line there). The notable things are that the coverage for the MLM estimators is often very bad but other than that the coverage for the cluster weighted estimators is generally good. The coverage rates for the person weighted estimators however are pretty bad across methods,it's either very low (meaning the SEs are being underestimated) or too high (meaning the SEs are being overestimated within the same methods. 

Description of Analysis:

*The first graph is a boxplot of the coverage by method. Coverage is the percentage of treatment effect estimates that fall in the 95% confidence interval. The vertical line is at 95%, which is what coverage should be.  

*The second graph is a boxplot of the normalized 95% confidence interval length by method.

## Is Low Degrees of Freedom Causing Problems because of Estimate Instability Driven or Bias  

Main Bullet Points:

*This is answering the question on page 35

*Low degrees of freedom is clearly causing problems because of estimate instability. There is clear increase in estimate instability for the low degrees of freedom DGPs (graph one) and no relation between degrees of freedom and mean bias (graph two).  

Description of Analysis:

*The first graph is scatter plot of the true estimate standard error across replications against the model degrees of freedom, graphed sepparately for each method


*The second graph is scatter plot of the mean bias across replications against the model degrees of freedom, graphed sepparately for each method

  plot_data,
  cols = c(inflate.s, inflate.f),
  names_to = "inflation_type",
  values_to = "inflation_value"
)

# Create nicer labels for the legend
plot_data_long$inflation_type <- factor(
  plot_data_long$inflation_type,
  levels = c("inflate.s", "inflate.f"),
  labels = c("Super Population", "Finite Population")
)



# Custom Box Plot
{ggplot(plot_data_long, aes(x = method_ordered, y = inflation_value, color = inflation_type)) + 
  # Add reference line at 1.0
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1.0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
  
  # Add faint min/max lines in background
  geom_linerange(
    stat = "summary",
    fun.data = function(x) {
      data.frame(ymin = min(x), ymax = max(x))
    },
    alpha = 0.2,
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  
  # Add 1% and 99% whiskers
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = function(x) {
      percentiles <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.01, 0.99))
      return(data.frame(ymin = percentiles[1], ymax = percentiles[2]))
    },
    geom = "errorbar",
    width = 0.5,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
  ) +
  
  # Add custom boxplot for 10% to 90%
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = function(x) {
      r <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9))
      names(r) <- c("ymin", "lower", "middle", "upper", "ymax")
      r
    },
    geom = "boxplot",
    alpha = 0.7,
    width = 0.5,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
  ) +
  
  # Labs and formatting
  labs(
    title = "Standard Error Inflation by Method",
    x = "",
    y = "Standard Error Inflation"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_flip() +
  
  # Use your own color mapping based on your data structure
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Super Population" = "darkblue", 
      "Finite Population" = "darkred"
    ),
    name = "Inflation Type"
  )
}

fin_plot.ICC <- create_custom_boxplot(
  sruns.finite.ICC, 
  "dif", 
  "How Much Closer the Estimated S.E. is to the True Super Population SE by Method, ICC > 0", 
  "Percentage Points",
  vline_at = 0
)
print(fin_plot.ICC) 

result <- create_top_n_table(
  data = sruns.finite,
  column_to_rank_by = "dif",
  methods_to_include = core.methods.se,
  n = 5,
  abs_value = TRUE,

)

#This plot is my attempt to show that the SE are mostly targeting super population
{
# Calculate the metrics for each method
comparison_data <- plot_data %>%
  group_by(method_ordered) %>%
  summarize(
    pct_s_closer_to_one = mean(round(abs(inflate.s - 1),2) < round(abs(inflate.f - 1),2)) * 100,
    pct_same = mean(round(abs(inflate.s - 1),2) == round(abs(inflate.f - 1),2)) * 100,
    pct_same_oreq = mean(round(abs(inflate.s - 1),2) <= round(abs(inflate.f - 1),2)) * 100
  ) %>%
  # Convert to long format for plotting
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(pct_s_closer_to_one, pct_same, pct_same_oreq),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "percentage"
  )

# Create nice labels for the metrics
comparison_data$metric <- factor(
  comparison_data$metric,
  levels = c("pct_s_closer_to_one", "pct_same", "pct_same_oreq"),
  labels = c("Estimated SE Closer to Super", "Super = Finite","Estimated SE Closer or Equal to Super")
)}

# Create the bar chart
ggplot(comparison_data, aes(x = method_ordered, y = percentage, fill = metric)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge(width = 0.9)) +
  #geom_hline(yintercept = 100, color="black")+
  labs(
    title = "Standard Errors are Mostly Targetting Super Population",
    x = "Method",
    y = "Percentage of Scenarios",
    fill = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  coord_flip()
